docs.title: What closing costs does a seller pay in South Florida?
docs.text: In South Florida, sellers customarily pay the real estate commission, the documentary stamp tax on the deed, the owner’s title insurance policy, prorated property taxes, an HOA estoppel fee where applicable, and a closing/settlement fee. docs.title: How much is the Florida documentary stamp tax when I sell?
docs.text: Florida charges documentary stamp tax on the deed at $0.70 per $100 of the sale price in most of the state. Miami-Dade County is different: the base rate is $0.60 per $100, plus a $0.45 per $100 surtax that applies to every property type except a single-family residence. So in Miami-Dade a $1,000,000 single-family home is about $6,000, while a $1,000,000 condo, multifamily, land, or commercial transfer is about $10,500. Confirm your figure with the closing agent (source: Florida Department of Revenue).

docs.title: Is the real estate commission a fixed rate in Florida?
docs.text: No. Commission is not set by law — it is negotiated as part of the listing agreement. A well-structured agreement addresses both the listing-side fee and compensation that motivates the buyer-agent network to show the property.

docs.title: How do I estimate my net proceeds?
docs.text: Start with the expected sale price, then subtract the mortgage payoff, commission, documentary stamp tax, owner’s title insurance, prorated taxes, and any HOA estoppel or settlement fees. A seller net sheet prepared for your specific property gives the most accurate figure; this article is general information, not a guarantee of any amount.

docs.title: What Florida taxes apply to a bridge loan or a HELOC?
docs.text: Two state taxes apply when a mortgage is recorded in Florida. Documentary stamp tax under section 201.08 is 35 cents on each $100 of the debt, and the nonrecurring intangible tax under section 199.133 is 2 mills per dollar. On a $500,000 closed-end bridge loan that is $1,750 plus $1,000, or $2,750, before lender fees. A line of credit is handled differently: intangible tax is paid on the maximum line at recording, while documentary stamp tax is paid on the initial debt and then on each advance. Your lender's closing disclosure shows the exact charges.

docs.title: Does a bridge loan count against my debt-to-income ratio when I buy before selling?
docs.text: Under the Fannie Mae Selling Guide, a bridge or swing loan used to buy a new principal residence before the current one is sold is a contingent liability that must be included in the debt-to-income ratio. Fannie Mae waives that requirement only when the lender has a fully executed sales contract for the current residence and confirmation that its financing contingencies have been cleared. Other loan programs and lenders apply their own rules, so the answer for a specific purchase should come from your lender.

docs.title: Is an extended closing safer than a post-closing occupancy agreement for Florida sellers?
docs.text: They protect different things. With an extended closing, the seller keeps ownership, insurance and risk until the later closing date, but the buyer must agree to wait and the longer contract period leaves more time for a financing or appraisal problem. With a post-closing occupancy, the sale closes on schedule and the seller stays under a separate written agreement, so occupancy terms, insurance and any escrowed funds must be settled before closing. Both should be drafted or reviewed by a Florida real estate attorney.

docs.title: What is the cheapest way to buy and sell a house at the same time in Florida without moving twice?
docs.text: Selling first usually adds the least cost, because it requires no new financing and so no interest or recording taxes on gap borrowing. The seller then negotiates an extended closing or a post-closing occupancy to stay in the home until the next purchase closes. Whether that is available depends on demand for the current home and the buyer's flexibility. Buying first with a bridge loan or a HELOC adds interest and Florida's taxes on the new mortgage, which on a $500,000 closed-end bridge loan total $2,750 before lender fees.

docs.text: Florida requires a milestone structural inspection for condominium buildings three habitable stories or more by December 31 of the year the building reaches 30 years of age, and every 10 years after that, and a structural integrity reserve study at least every 10 years. Buildings that need critical repairs, failed a mandatory inspection or face certain litigation can be ineligible for Fannie Mae financing, which removes many financed buyers. Sellers in those buildings should expect more cash buyers and should prepare the association's documents before pricing.

docs.text: Obtain a current four-point inspection and a wind-mitigation report before listing, so buyers can secure insurance quotes early, and set the asking price from recent comparable sales and current neighborhood absorption rather than from the highest past sale. With 30-year mortgage rates averaging 7.11% in mid-November 2026, financed buyers are price-sensitive, and listings priced above the evidence tend to sit.

docs.title: Should I sell my South Florida home now?

docs.title: Do you have to disclose flooding when selling a house in Florida?
docs.text: Yes. docs.title: What does the Florida flood disclosure form ask a seller?
docs.text: The form opens with a statement that homeowners' insurance policies do not include coverage for damage resulting from floods. The seller then checks boxes stating whether they have knowledge of flooding that damaged the property during their ownership, whether they filed a flood damage claim with an insurance provider, including the National Flood Insurance Program, and whether they received assistance for flood damage, including from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The form also defines flooding for the purpose of those answers.

docs.title: When must a Florida seller give the buyer the flood disclosure?
docs.text: The statute requires the disclosure at or before the time the sales contract is executed. In practice, sellers prepare it with the listing file so a buyer reads it before making an offer. A buyer who reads the answers early prices them into the offer, while information that surfaces after a contract is signed tends to reopen the negotiation. The exact sequence for a given sale is worth confirming with the closing attorney or title agent.

docs.title: Does homeowners insurance cover flood damage in Florida?
docs.text: The statutory flood disclosure form states that homeowners' insurance policies do not include coverage for damage resulting from floods, and it encourages the buyer to discuss separate flood insurance with the buyer's own insurance agent. Whether a particular property has flood coverage, and what it costs, depends on the policy in force and the insurer. Sellers should keep the declarations page of any current flood policy in the listing file, because buyers and their insurers routinely ask for it.

docs.title: Florida Homestead and Save Our Homes Portability
docs.text: Florida's Homestead Exemption and Save Our Homes cap protect homeowners — and portability lets you carry the benefit to your next home. Here is how it works. docs.title: What is the Florida Homestead Exemption worth?
docs.text: Under Florida Statute §196.031, the Homestead Exemption removes up to $50,000 from the assessed value of your permanent residence — the first $25,000 applies to all property taxes, and an additional $25,000 (on assessed value between $50,000 and $75,000) applies to non-school taxes. You must apply with your county property appraiser, generally by March 1.

docs.title: What is the Save Our Homes cap?
docs.text: Save Our Homes limits how much the assessed value of a homesteaded property can rise each year to 3% or the change in the Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower. Over time this can keep your taxable value well below market value.

docs.title: Can I transfer my Save Our Homes benefit to a new home?
docs.text: Yes. Portability lets you transfer up to $500,000 of your accumulated Save Our Homes benefit to a new homestead within Florida, using form DR-501T filed alongside the new Homestead Exemption application.

docs.title: How long do I have to establish a new homestead for portability?
docs.text: A 2020 constitutional amendment extended the window to three tax years following the year you abandoned your prior homestead. Confirm timing with your county property appraiser.

docs.title: The $250,000 / $500,000 Home Sale Capital Gains Exclusion

Key sections: The $250,000 / $500,000 Home Sale Capital Gains Exclusion — How It Works for Primary Residences · What the exclusion actually covers · The two core tests: ownership and use · The "once every two years" limit · Partial exclusions

docs.title: How much capital gain can I exclude when I sell my home?
docs.text: Under IRC Section 121, a single filer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on the sale of a primary residence, and a married couple filing jointly may exclude up to $500,000, if the ownership and use tests are met.

docs.title: What are the requirements to qualify?
docs.text: Generally, during the five years ending on the sale date you must have owned the home for at least two years and lived in it as your main home for at least two years. The periods need not be continuous.

docs.title: Does the exclusion apply to a rental or second home?
docs.text: No. The exclusion is for a primary residence. Property used as a rental may have depreciation that must be recaptured, and second homes are treated differently. Consult a tax professional.

docs.title: Can I use the home-sale exclusion more than once?
docs.text: Generally you cannot claim the exclusion if you used it on the sale of another home within the two years before the current sale.

docs.title: What is FIRPTA and how does it affect foreign sellers?
docs.text: FIRPTA is a federal law requiring the buyer to withhold a percentage of the sale price when purchasing U.S. real property from a foreign person, remitted to the IRS toward the seller’s potential tax. docs.title: Do I need to be in Florida to close on my sale?

docs.title: What is a post-closing occupancy agreement?
docs.text: It is a written addendum to the purchase contract under which the buyer takes ownership at closing but the seller remains in the property for an agreed short period afterward, governed by terms such as duration, an occupancy fee, and a security deposit.

docs.title: How long can a seller stay after closing?
docs.text: These arrangements are meant to be short. Because owner-occupant buyers’ lenders typically expect the buyer to move in within about 60 days, longer periods must be checked against the buyer’s mortgage terms.

docs.title: Does the seller pay to stay after closing?
docs.text: Usually yes — the addendum commonly sets a daily or monthly occupancy fee, often approximating the buyer’s carrying costs, plus a refundable security deposit. The terms are negotiated as part of the contract.

docs.title: Who pays the special assessment when you sell a condo in Florida?
docs.text: Florida law settles who the association can collect from, not how the seller and buyer split the cost. Under section 718.116 of the Florida Statutes, a new owner is jointly and severally liable with the previous owner for unpaid assessments that came due up to the transfer of title. How an approved assessment that is not yet due is divided is negotiated in the purchase contract: the seller may pay it at closing, the buyer may assume the remaining installments, or the parties may agree on a credit or a price adjustment. Have a Florida real estate attorney review that contract language.

docs.title: Can I sell my Florida condo if there is a special assessment?
docs.text: Yes. Nothing in the Florida condominium statute prevents an owner from selling a unit while a special assessment is pending or being paid in installments. The assessment will appear in the association's estoppel certificate, which must itemize special assessments owed and those scheduled to come due, and the association holds a lien on the unit to secure payment. The practical work is documenting the assessment early, deciding how it will be allocated, and pricing the unit against comparable sales in the same building.

docs.title: What does a condo estoppel certificate show about special assessments?
docs.text: Under section 718.116, the estoppel certificate must give an itemized list of all assessments, special assessments and other moneys owed on the date it is issued, and an itemized list of additional assessments and special assessments scheduled to become due during its effective period. The association must issue it within 10 business days after a written or electronic request. A certificate delivered by hand or electronically has a 30-day effective period, and one sent by regular mail has a 35-day effective period.

docs.title: What documents must a Florida condo seller give the buyer?
docs.text: Under section 718.503, as published in the 2025 Florida Statutes, a buyer from an owner who is not the developer is entitled, at the seller's expense, to current copies of the declaration, articles, bylaws and rules, the annual financial statement and budget, the milestone inspection summary where applicable, the latest structural integrity reserve study or a statement that none has been completed, the turnover inspection report where applicable, and the Frequently Asked Questions document, plus a governance form. If they are not delivered in time, the buyer may void the contract during a 7-day period, excluding weekends and legal holidays.

docs.title: What must a Florida listing agreement include?
docs.text: Section 475.25(1)(r) of the Florida Statutes requires a written listing agreement to include a definite expiration date, a description of the property, the price and terms, the fee or commission, and the proper signature of each owner. The owner must receive a legible, signed copy, and the agreement may not require the owner to notify the broker of an intention to cancel after the expiration date. The commercial terms beyond those minimums are negotiated between the owner and the brokerage.

docs.title: Can a Florida listing agreement renew automatically?
docs.text: The statute says a written listing agreement may contain no provision requiring the owner to notify the broker of an intention to cancel the listing after its definite expiration date. In practice, that rules out a clause that keeps the listing alive unless the owner objects in writing. An owner who wants to continue after expiration can sign an extension; one who does not simply lets the date pass. Specific contract questions belong with a Florida real estate attorney.

docs.title: Is my listing agreement with the agent or with the brokerage?
docs.text: With the brokerage. Under section 475.42(1)(d) of the Florida Statutes, a sales associate may not collect a commission, deposit or other money in a brokerage transaction except in the name of the employing broker and with the broker's express consent. The agreement therefore names the brokerage, and the brokerage's supervision and escrow practices stand behind the sale, even though the owner usually works day to day with an individual agent.

docs.title: What is the difference between a transaction broker and a single agent in Florida?
docs.text: Under section 475.278, a transaction broker provides limited, nonfiduciary representation and may assist the buyer, the seller or both, with duties such as honest dealing, accounting for funds and limited confidentiality. A single agent represents only one party as a fiduciary and adds loyalty, full confidentiality, obedience and full disclosure. Florida presumes transaction brokerage unless a single agent relationship is established in writing, and dual agency is prohibited.

docs.title: What is a pocket listing or private listing in South Florida?
docs.text: A pocket listing or private listing is a property marketed without full exposure on the MLS. In South Florida, the Miami MLS rules call the formal version an office exclusive: the owner, advised in writing of the benefits of the MLS, instructs the listing broker in writing not to distribute the listing publicly or to other MLS participants. The listing is still filed with the MLS, showings are permitted, and the seller signs an authorization form acknowledging the exposure being waived.

docs.title: Should I sell my house off-market or list it on the MLS?
docs.text: It depends on the objective. Limited exposure can fit an owner with a security, privacy or access concern, or a property that is not ready to show. When the objective is price, the Miami MLS seller form for office exclusive listings is direct: restricting marketing limits broad access to information and may affect the sale price, and it may reduce the number of potential buyers. Ask the listing agent which status is proposed and read the form first. This is general information, not legal or financial advice.

docs.title: Does a private listing sell for more or less than an MLS listing?
docs.text: Published studies disagree. A national brokerage's own study found privately pre-marketed homes sold for more, while a listing portal's study released in May 2026 and an MLS-sponsored analysis found off-MLS sales brought less. An academic study of Dallas–Fort Worth sales found a premium in older data that was no longer statistically significant after the Clear Cooperation Policy took effect. None of these measures a specific South Florida property, and none predicts the outcome of a sale. A pricing analysis of current comparables is the relevant evidence.

docs.title: Can I keep my home off public websites and still have it in the MLS?
docs.text: Under the Miami MLS, yes. The association's seller form describes an option labeled Active – Internet N, in which information about the property is not publicly displayed or distributed on the internet or third-party websites but is still shared with other MLS participants and subscribers, who can share it with their own customers. An owner may also ask in the listing agreement that the address be withheld from online publication to third parties. Confirm the current rule with the listing agent before signing.

docs.title: Can I switch from an office exclusive to a full MLS listing later?
docs.text: Yes. The Miami MLS seller authorization form for office exclusive listings states that the seller may, at any time, instruct the listing broker to enter the listing into the MLS. While a property is held as an office exclusive, days on market do not accrue under the MLS rules. Owners should agree in advance, in writing, on the point at which the property moves to full distribution if the private period does not produce an acceptable offer. Contract questions belong with a Florida real estate attorney.

docs.title: What is a 1031 exchange?
docs.text: A 1031 exchange (IRC Section 1031) lets an investor defer capital gains tax by reinvesting the proceeds from the sale of investment or business real property into like-kind real property.

docs.title: Does a 1031 exchange apply to my primary residence?
docs.text: No. Section 1031 applies only to real property held for investment or business use. The sale of a primary residence is instead governed by the Section 121 exclusion.

docs.title: What are the 1031 exchange deadlines?
docs.text: You have 45 calendar days from the sale to identify replacement property in writing, and 180 calendar days to close on it. These periods run concurrently and are not routinely extended.

docs.title: Does a 1031 exchange eliminate capital gains tax?
docs.text: No. It defers the tax — potentially indefinitely if you keep exchanging — but does not erase it. A qualified intermediary must hold the proceeds for the exchange to qualify.

docs.title: Does Florida portability transfer if I move to another state?
docs.text: No. The Save Our Homes assessment benefit and portability apply only to a Florida homestead. When you establish residency in another state, that accumulated benefit is left behind. Portability can only be transferred to another home within Florida.

docs.title: Do I still get the capital gains exclusion if I move out of Florida?
docs.text: The federal IRC Section 121 exclusion (up to $250,000 single / $500,000 married filing jointly) follows you regardless of where you move, provided you meet the ownership and use tests on the home you are selling. Documented improvements raise your basis and reduce taxable gain. Confirm eligibility with a CPA, especially when changing state residency.

docs.title: How can I avoid moving twice when relocating?
docs.text: A post-closing occupancy agreement (a seller leaseback) lets you remain in the home for a defined short period after closing under agreed terms, which can turn two moves into one. It is negotiated as part of the contract and has constraints tied to the buyer’s financing, so plan it early.

docs.title: What is the difference between listing a home online and activating the market?
docs.text: Listing online makes a property findable by buyers already searching that price band and starts the days-on-market clock. Activating the market is the deliberate work of positioning a correctly priced property in front of qualified buyers and the agents who represent them — through MLS distribution, buyer-agent outreach, and international and relocation channels — before days-on-market begins to work against the seller.

docs.title: Does more online exposure guarantee a higher sale price?
docs.text: No. No agent can guarantee a price or timeline. Broad distribution creates a structural advantage — more qualified buyers and agents become aware of the property — but the result still depends on pricing supported by current MLS data, condition, presentation, timing, and negotiation.

docs.title: What questions should a South Florida seller ask before listing?
docs.text: Beyond "what is my home worth," a seller should ask who will actually see the property, how it will be positioned against current competition, which buyers and agents will be activated, what market data supports the price, and what the plan is after the sale — for example downsizing, relocating, a 1031 exchange, or porting a homestead benefit.

docs.title: How much can a married couple exclude from capital gains when selling a primary home?
docs.text: Under IRC Section 121, a married couple filing jointly can exclude up to $500,000 of gain on the sale of a primary residence if they meet the ownership and use tests — generally owning and living in the home at least two of the five years before the sale. Documented capital improvements add to your cost basis and can further reduce taxable gain. Confirm your situation with a CPA.

docs.title: How is Florida portability calculated when you downsize?
docs.text: When you buy a less expensive home, Florida transfers a proportional share of your Save Our Homes benefit: (new market value ÷ old market value) × your accumulated benefit, up to $500,000. For example, moving from a $1.1M home to a $550,000 home transfers 50% of the benefit. Your county property appraiser calculates the exact figure.

docs.title: Can downsizing eliminate a mortgage payment?
docs.text: Often, yes. If net sale proceeds exceed the price of the replacement home, a seller can purchase the next home outright and remove the mortgage principal and interest entirely — typically the largest line in a monthly housing budget — while also lowering property taxes through portability and reducing insurance on a smaller home.

docs.title: Does a higher sale price change the whole downsizing plan?
docs.text: Yes. Net proceeds drive every later step — the cash available for the next home, the reserve left over, and the monthly cost reset. Because the realized sale price depends heavily on how the home is positioned and distributed, the sale strategy is the most controllable variable in the plan.

docs.title: Does Amendment 3 change Save Our Homes or portability in Florida?
docs.text: County property appraisers say it does not. The Volusia County and Leon County offices both state that Amendment 3 does not eliminate or replace Save Our Homes and does not change Florida's portability provisions. Annual increases in a homestead's assessment remain limited to the lower of 3% or the change in the Consumer Price Index, and portability still allows up to $500,000 of the Save Our Homes difference to move to a new homestead established inside the three-year window. Ask your county property appraiser how the rules apply to your parcel.

docs.title: If I sell my Florida home and buy another, which homestead exemption applies under Amendment 3?
docs.text: The amendment's smaller, newcomer tier is written for a person who had not maintained a permanent residence in Florida as of December 31, 2026. County appraisers say permanent Florida residents as of that date are eligible for the larger amounts, including residents who buy later and apply for homestead. The text has no sentence addressing an owner who sells one homestead and establishes another, and implementing legislation is still required. Confirm your situation with the property appraiser in the county of the next home before you close.

docs.title: Will I need to wait five years for the larger homestead exemption?
docs.text: The five-year rule is aimed at newcomers. Under the text, a person who had not maintained a permanent residence in Florida as of December 31, 2026 is exempt up to $50,000 for non-school levies and reaches the larger amount beginning with the fifth year of exemption. County appraisers describe this as four years of homestead exemption, with eligibility on January 1 of the fifth year. Owners who were permanent Florida residents by that date are described by the same offices as eligible for the larger amounts beginning in 2027.

docs.title: Do I need to do anything to qualify for the Amendment 3 exemption in 2027?
docs.text: It depends on your situation, and guidance is still developing. The Leon County Property Appraiser says additional guidance may be necessary to determine whether owners will need to provide documentation or take other steps for the increased exemption. A newly purchased home always needs its own homestead application; the Broward County Property Appraiser lists March 1, 2027 as the end of the timely filing period for a 2027 homestead exemption. Check your own county property appraiser's site for current instructions.

docs.title: When does Amendment 3 show up on a Florida property tax bill?
docs.text: Not on the 2026 bill. Amendment 3 takes effect on January 1, 2027. The Leon County Property Appraiser states that it does not affect 2026 property tax bills and that the changes will first be reflected on the August 2027 notices of proposed property taxes and the tax bills mailed in November 2027. The non-school homestead exemption is up to $150,000 of assessed value for 2027 and up to $250,000 beginning in 2028, while the school-levy exemption stays at up to $25,000.

docs.title: What housing costs can downsizing actually reduce?
docs.text: Beyond a smaller mortgage (or none, if you buy the next home outright), downsizing can lower property taxes, homeowner/windstorm/flood insurance, HOA or CDD fees, maintenance and major-system replacement costs, and monthly utilities. It can also free equity that was otherwise sitting idle in an over-large home.

docs.title: Do I lose my Homestead tax benefits if I downsize?
docs.text: Not if you stay within Florida. You can claim a new Homestead Exemption on your next permanent residence and use portability to carry up to $500,000 of your accumulated Save Our Homes benefit. When downsizing, the benefit transfers proportionally — (new market value ÷ old market value) × your benefit — as calculated by your county property appraiser.

docs.title: Can downsizing eliminate my mortgage payment entirely?
docs.text: Often, yes. If the net proceeds from your sale exceed the price of the replacement home, you may be able to purchase the next home with cash and remove the principal-and-interest payment — typically the largest recurring housing cost — while keeping a cash reserve.

docs.title: Are lower monthly costs guaranteed after downsizing?
docs.text: No. Savings depend on choices: high HOA dues can offset reduced maintenance, and a coastal condo may carry insurance comparable to a larger inland home. The goal is a net reduction in predictable monthly cost, which is why a property-specific review of taxes, insurance, dues, and reserves matters before you commit.
